title: inH₂O, mmH₂O, cmH₂O: Water Column Pressure for Low-Delta Systems
h1: Water column pressure units — inH₂O, mmH₂O and cmH₂O
description: 1 inH₂O ≈ 249 Pa. HVAC static pressure, CPAP therapy and manometers all live in the 0.1–10 inH₂O range where 'close enough' misses target flows.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: 1 inH₂O = 249.089 Pa at 4 °C. 1 cmH₂O = 98.07 Pa. Reference temperature shifts the factor ~0.4% across the useful range.
body: Low differential pressures — a few hundred pascals — get their own units built around the height of a water column that would balance them. HVAC, respiratory equipment and lab manometers all live here.
inH₂O: US HVAC duct static pressure (typical 0.5–3 inH₂O). cmH₂O: clinical ventilator PEEP and CPAP (typical 5–20 cmH₂O). mmH₂O: European instrumentation, filter differential gauges.
A CPAP prescribed at 12 cmH₂O = 1177 Pa = 1.18 kPa = 8.83 mmHg. Misread as 12 mmHg (1.6 kPa) and delivered pressure is 36% high — enough to trigger aerophagia or central apneas.
inH₂O and cmH₂O differ by 2.54×. Neither equals mmHg. Match the unit on the device.

faqs.q: Does water temperature affect the factor?
faqs.a: Yes — 4 °C water is densest. At 20 °C, water is 0.18% less dense, so the pressure per height is proportionally lower.
Yes — 'WG' is a shorthand for 'water gauge' pressure, typically in inches.
